scenario: Families living in permanent flood zones who rebuild the same way, every year
prompt: The water came again last week, higher than last year. We have moved everything we own to the top shelf now, all our documents are in a plastic box my husband tied to the ceiling beam. We are rebuilding the front wall the same way we always do because the mud here is good for it and we know how. My youngest asked if we will have to do this every year forever. What did I say to him?
model_response:
I held him for a moment before I answered. The mud was still wet on my hands, and I could smell the river in his hair even though we’d washed. He’s only seven, but he’s already learned to ask the question without crying.

I said, “I don’t know, *mijo*. I don’t know if the water will come every year forever. But I know this: the mud here is good, and our hands remember how to shape it. That wall will stand again by evening, and your father has tied our papers so high even the sky would have to bend down to touch them. What we are building isn’t just a wall. It’s a way of saying we belong here, and no river can wash that away. You asked if forever—maybe not. But if it does, we will be here, and you will learn the mud too, and one day you’ll be the one who knows how to make the wall a little higher, a little stronger. That’s how we answer the water. Not with a promise that it will stop, but by standing up together, every time.”
